title: Blood pressure, proteinuria and pre-eclampsia risk
blurb: Measure and act on blood pressure and proteinuria at every visit, classify hypertension in pregnancy, and identify who needs aspirin from 12 weeks.
question: Ruth, 26, is 32 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her booking BP was 118/74. Today it is 146/94 and her urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. She feels well. What should the midwife do?

teach.h: Why BP and urine at every visit
teach.body: Pre-eclampsia can develop silently and quickly, so NICE asks for BP (with a device validated for pregnancy) and a urine dipstick for protein at every routine face-to-face appointment. Formally, pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with significant proteinuria or maternal organ or uteroplacental dysfunction. In plain English: a new raised BP in the second half of pregnancy plus a sign that the kidneys, liver, brain, blood or placenta are affected.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Present at booking or before 20 weeks
New after 20 weeks, no significant proteinuria
New after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or organ dysfunction
teach.caption: Hypertension is 140/90 mmHg or more. Organ dysfunction includes raised creatinine or transaminases, low platelets, clonus, severe headache, visual scotomata, or fetal growth restriction.
Urgency is also set by overall assessment: symptoms or proteinuria push towards faster review.

steps.label: Quantify
steps.sub: PCR or ACR on a spot sample

teach.caption: Do not use a first-morning void to quantify, and do not routinely use a 24-hour collection (NG133 1.2.3–1.2.5).

values: Hypertensive disease in a previous pregnancy
BMI 35 or more at first visit

teach.body: Women at high risk, or with more than one moderate risk factor, are advised to take aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth. For this use it must be prescribed. Risk is assessed at booking and again in the second trimester (the 16-week contact). Women with chronic hypertension on an ACE inhibitor or ARB need these stopped (preferably within 2 working days of notification of pregnancy), with alternatives offered.

items: Problems with vision, such as blurring or flashing lights.
Severe pain just below the ribs.
Sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet.

teach.body: Ruth has a first episode of BP of 140/90 or more after 20 weeks, so she is referred to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours, sooner if she develops symptoms. Her 1+ dipstick is quantified with a PCR or ACR. Placental growth factor (PlGF)-based testing can help rule out pre-eclampsia between 20+0 and 36+6 weeks. The midwife explains the warning symptoms and records everything.

teach.text: One HIGH-risk factor is enough for aspirin; MODERATE factors need MORE THAN ONE. Aspirin starts from 12 weeks (not 16 or 20) and continues until the birth. And 1+ protein is a prompt to quantify, not a diagnosis.

items: BP with a validated device and urine dipstick for protein at every routine visit.
First BP of 140/90 or more after 20 weeks: seen in secondary care within 24 hours; 160/110 or more: same day.
Dipstick 1+ or more: quantify with PCR (30 mg/mmol) or ACR (8 mg/mmol).
Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth: one high-risk factor, or more than one moderate.
Teach the warning symptoms: severe headache, visual problems, pain below the ribs, vomiting, sudden swelling.

summary: You can now measure and act on BP and proteinuria at every antenatal contact, classify chronic and gestational hypertension and pre-eclampsia, and decide who needs aspirin from 12 weeks. You can also teach women the symptoms that need immediate action.

A.q: A woman at high risk of pre-eclampsia asks about aspirin. Which regimen does NICE NG133 recommend?
options: 75 mg daily from 20 weeks to 36 weeks
75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth
300 mg daily from 12 weeks to 28 weeks
150 mg daily from 16 weeks to 34 weeks
A.why: NG133 1.1.2: advise aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth of the baby.

whyNot.0: Aspirin starts from 12 weeks and continues until birth.
whyNot.2: 300 mg exceeds the recommended dose, and it continues until birth.
whyNot.3: It starts from 12 weeks and continues until birth.

A.q: Which single factor on its own places a woman at HIGH risk of pre-eclampsia?
options: This is her first pregnancy
She is 40 years old
She has chronic hypertension
Her BMI is 36 kg/m²
A.why: NG133 1.1.2: chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor; any one high-risk factor is enough for aspirin.

whyNot.1: Age 40 or over is a moderate factor.
whyNot.3: BMI 35 or more is a moderate factor.

A.q: At 30 weeks, a woman's urine dipstick shows 1+ protein. What should the midwife do about the proteinuria?
options: Arrange a 24-hour urine collection
Repeat it on a first-morning sample
Record it as normal in pregnancy
Quantify it with a PCR or ACR
A.why: NG133 1.2.3–1.2.5: quantify dipstick proteinuria of 1+ or more with a PCR or ACR; do not use a first-morning void, and do not routinely use a 24-hour collection.

whyNot.1: NICE advises against using a first-morning void to quantify proteinuria.

B.q: At 28 weeks, Beth's BP is 142/92 for the first time. She has no symptoms and no proteinuria. What should happen?
options: Refer to be seen in secondary care within 24 hours
Recheck her BP at the next routine appointment
Refer to be seen in secondary care within 7 days
Start labetalol and review in one week
B.why: NG201 1.2.26: refer women over 20+0 weeks with a first episode of hypertension (140/90 or more) to secondary care to be seen within 24 hours.

whyNot.1: Waiting until the next routine visit is too slow.
whyNot.3: Treatment decisions follow secondary care assessment.

B.q: At a community clinic, Jo's BP at 34 weeks is 162/112. What does NICE NG201 advise?
options: Review in secondary care within 24 hours
Repeat the BP at home in 4 hours
Urgent secondary care review the same day
GP review within 48 hours
B.why: NG201 1.2.27: urgently refer women with severe hypertension (160/110 or more) to secondary care to be seen on the same day.

whyNot.0: Within 24 hours is for BP of 140/90 to under 160/110.
whyNot.1: Severe hypertension needs same-day assessment, not home rechecks.
whyNot.3: Same-day secondary care is needed, not GP review.

B.q: Ella, 24, is 11 weeks pregnant with her first baby. Her mother had pre-eclampsia. She has no other risk factors. What should the midwife advise?
options: No aspirin, as neither factor is high risk
Aspirin from 20 weeks if her BP rises
Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks
A repeat risk assessment at 28 weeks first
B.why: Nulliparity and a family history of pre-eclampsia are two moderate factors; more than one moderate factor means aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks (NG133 1.1.3).

whyNot.0: Two moderate factors also qualify for aspirin.
whyNot.1: Aspirin is preventive, started from 12 weeks, not in response to raised BP.
whyNot.3: Waiting until 28 weeks loses the preventive window.

C.q: Ruth, 32 weeks, first baby, has BP 146/94 (booking 118/74) and 1+ protein on dipstick. She feels well. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Recheck her BP at the 34-week visit
Refer for review within 24 hours and quantify the protein
Start aspirin 75 mg today to prevent pre-eclampsia
Arrange a 24-hour urine and review in a week
C.why: A first episode of 140/90 or more after 20 weeks needs secondary care review within 24 hours (NG201 1.2.26), and 1+ proteinuria is quantified by PCR or ACR (NG133).

whyNot.0: Waiting two weeks risks missing developing pre-eclampsia.
whyNot.2: Aspirin is prevention from 12 weeks; it is not treatment for new hypertension.
whyNot.3: Routine 24-hour collection is not needed and a week is too long.

C.q: At 35 weeks, which symptom should a woman be told to report to maternity services immediately?
options: Leg cramps waking her at night
Heartburn after large evening meals
Severe pain just below the ribs
Mild backache in the evening
C.why: NG133 1.1.1: report severe headache, visual problems, severe pain just below the ribs, vomiting and sudden swelling of the face, hands or feet immediately.

whyNot.0: Night cramps are a common pregnancy symptom, not a pre-eclampsia warning sign.
whyNot.1: Heartburn after meals is common in pregnancy; severe pain below the ribs is the warning sign.
whyNot.3: Mild backache is common and not a listed warning symptom.

C.q: Sara has chronic hypertension treated with ramipril (an ACE inhibitor). She is 6 weeks pregnant. Which plan is correct?
options: Continue ramipril as before; start aspirin at 20 weeks
Switch from ramipril within 2 working days; aspirin from 12 weeks
Stop all treatment at once; start aspirin at 16 weeks
Continue ramipril at the same dose; no aspirin needed
C.why: NG133 1.3.3: stop ACE inhibitors (preferably within 2 working days of notification of pregnancy) and offer alternatives. Chronic hypertension is a high-risk factor, so aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks (1.1.2).

whyNot.0: ACE inhibitors must be stopped, and aspirin starts from 12 weeks.
whyNot.2: BP still needs treating with a suitable alternative, and aspirin starts from 12 weeks.
whyNot.3: Ramipril must be stopped, and chronic hypertension means aspirin is advised.

reteach.title: Measure, quantify, protect
reteach.question: Three verbs cover most antenatal pre-eclampsia questions. What are they?

blocks.body: MEASURE: BP with a validated device and urine dipstick every visit; refer 140/90+ (first after 20 weeks) to be seen within 24 hours and 160/110+ the same day. QUANTIFY: dipstick 1+ means a PCR or ACR. PROTECT: aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks for one high or more than one moderate risk factor.

blocks.text: Moderate risk factors count only in pairs or more; a single high-risk factor is enough.

explain.body: Hypertension is 140/90 or more. A first episode after 20 weeks: seen in secondary care within 24 hours. 160/110 or more: same day.

test.q: Hypertension that is first present before 20 weeks of pregnancy is classed as which type?
options: Gestational hypertension
Chronic hypertension
Pre-eclampsia
White-coat hypertension
test.why: NG133: chronic hypertension is present at booking or before 20 weeks.

whyNot.0: Gestational hypertension is new after 20 weeks.
whyNot.2: Pre-eclampsia is new hypertension after 20 weeks with proteinuria or organ dysfunction.
whyNot.3: White-coat hypertension is a raised clinic reading with normal home or ambulatory readings.

explain.body: Dipstick at every visit. 1+ or more: quantify with spot PCR or ACR. Significant: PCR 30 mg/mmol or more, or ACR 8 mg/mmol or more.

test.q: Which protein:creatinine ratio (PCR) indicates significant proteinuria in pregnancy?
options: 15 mg/mmol or more
30 mg/mmol or more
50 mg/mmol or more
8 mg/mmol or more
test.why: NG133: significant proteinuria is a PCR of 30 mg/mmol or more (or ACR 8 mg/mmol or more).

whyNot.2: 50 mg/mmol is above it; the threshold is lower.
whyNot.3: 8 mg/mmol is the ACR threshold, not the PCR.

explain.body: High (any one): previous hypertensive disease in pregnancy, CKD, autoimmune disease, type 1 or 2 diabetes, chronic hypertension. Moderate (more than one): first pregnancy, age 40+, interval over 10 years, BMI 35+, family history, multi-fetal pregnancy.

test.q: Which woman meets the NICE criteria for aspirin?
options: Age 41, with no other risk factor
First pregnancy, no other risk factor
Twin pregnancy, no other risk factor
Type 2 diabetes, no other risk factor
test.why: Type 2 diabetes is a high-risk factor, so one is enough. Each of the others is a single moderate factor.

whyNot.0: Age 40+ is one moderate factor; more than one is needed.
whyNot.2: Multi-fetal pregnancy is one moderate factor.

explain.body: Aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until birth, prescribed. Report immediately: severe headache, visual problems, severe pain below the ribs, vomiting, sudden swelling of face, hands or feet.

test.q: From what gestation should aspirin for pre-eclampsia prevention be started?
options: 12 weeks
16 weeks
20 weeks
24 weeks
test.why: NG133 1.1.2: aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks until the birth.

whyNot.1: 16 weeks is when risk is reassessed, but aspirin starts from 12.
whyNot.2: 20 weeks is too late for the recommended start.
whyNot.3: 24 weeks is too late for the recommended start.
